newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientists report new deep space mystery.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientists report new deep space mystery.

text.p: Scientists reported on Tuesday never-before-seen repeat bursts of gamma radiation in deep space, adding mystery to a phenomenon little understood despite 25 years of research.

Four separate high energy bursts -- two groups of two each in rapid succession -- were detected Oct. 27 and 29 by an earth-orbiting observatory launched in 1991 from the Space Shuttle Atlantis, NASA said.
The development was detailed at an astrophysics symposium in Chicago.
"The repeated bursts are unlike any of the other 1,700 gamma-ray bursts observed by (the satellite device)," the announcement said.

The orbiting observatory usually detects about one gamma-ray burst per day, lasting from 10 to 30 seconds, and apparently randomly distributed. The causes of the bursts and the distances of their origin are still being debated by scientists despite a quarter century of study, it added.
The development is a "puzzling new twist" in gamma radiation study, the space agency said.
The repeat nature of the bursts is "what makes these recent events so unusual," said Charles Meegan of the Marshall Space Flight Centre.
"They came right after one another, about two days apart and all from the same part of the sky. Moreover, the last one was much longer than usual, lasting 23 minutes," he added.

Valerie Connaughton, an astrophysicist with the same centre, said "It would be unlikely that this actually happened by chance" but researchers do not know if the events were produced by just one object in space or several.

"Some astronomers argue for an explanation that the origin of these bursts is fairly local, just outside our own galaxy," added Gerald Fishman, principal investigator for the observatory project, which is known as the Burst and Transient Source Experiment.
"But most believe that bursts come from remote parts of the universe, at cosmological distances of a billion light years or more," he added.
